claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The internal lamellar boundaries strongly obstruct dislocation motion.
Dislocation obstruction at the internal boundaries causes pile-ups and local stress concentrations.
Boundary-associated pile-ups and stress concentrations cause microcracking and brittle tensile failure in the untreated alloy.
Targeted low-temperature annealing can trigger an interfacial complexion transition or controlled solute segregation along the lamellar boundaries.
A sufficiently low annealing temperature can modify interfacial chemistry without coarsening the lamellae.
The annealed boundaries will contain segregated solute species and have a reduced interfacial barrier.
The modified interfacial complexion will facilitate easier dislocation transmission across lamellar interfaces.
Lower barriers to dislocation transmission will reduce dislocation accumulation at the lamellar boundaries.
Reduced dislocation accumulation will diminish local stress concentrations and prevent microcrack initiation.
Preservation of the fine lamellar architecture contributes to high strength.
The treated alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature tensile ductility and less brittle behavior than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will maintain or modestly improve strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The proposed benefits occur only within a limited annealing regime that promotes an interfacial transition without changing the bulk microstructure.
The response may depend on annealing temperature, duration, alloy composition, and minor compositional changes.
Mechanical performance is to be evaluated by standardized tensile testing at room temperature.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome allows strength merely to be maintained or modestly improved, whereas the falsification rule describes the hypothesis as requiring improvement in both ductility and strength. The latter is a stricter outcome than the stated prediction.
